they mainly report bias perceptions and general skepticism.[31][32][33] The statement about AI screening being opaque and applicants not understanding why they were rejected is an interpretive extension, not a directly reported survey finding in the accessible documentation.","fact_id":"applicant_usa_transparency_concern_pew_asa","independent_source_name":"American Staffing Association Workforce Monitor – \"AI in Hiring\" page","independent_source_url":"https://americanstaffing.net/asa-workforce-monitor/ai-in-hiring/","verdict":"PARTIALLY_CONFIRMED"},{"explanation":"The Nature portfolio article \"Ethics and discrimination in artificial intelligence-enabled recruitment practices\" reports that AI-enabled recruitment can introduce **algorithmic bias resulting in discriminatory hiring practices based on gender, race, color, and personality traits**, and discusses risks that candidates may be disadvantaged by automated screening.[16][17] It frames these concerns as raised by stakeholders including job applicants and civil society and notes that such systems can perpetrate discrimination.[16][17] While the accessible abstract does not spell out in detail that candidates \"cannot contest\" decisions, it does emphasize discriminatory risks in automated hiring, consistent with the core of the fact.","fact_id":"applicant_global_discrimination_concern_nature_2023","independent_source_name":"Nature Humanities and Social Sciences Communications – \"Ethics and discrimination in artificial intelligence-enabled recruitment practices\"","independent_source_url":"https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-023-02079-x","verdict":"CONFIRMED"},{"explanation":"Coverage of the ASA Workforce Monitor and subsequent industry commentary (e.g., StaffingHub’s \"49% of Job Seekers Think Your AI Screening Is Biased. Here’s the documentation that answers them\") describe that job seekers are concerned about AI and that recruiters should provide documentation to address these concerns.[31][32][33] However, independent sources do **not** clearly document survey questions or results specifically about job seekers feeling pressure to \"beat\" or \"game\" AI or heavily tailor resumes to algorithms; that language appears mainly in opinion/guidance pieces rather than as a reported survey statistic.[33] Thus the general anxiety about AI is supported, but the specific \"game the system\" pressure is not directly confirmed as a survey finding.","fact_id":"applicant_usa_fear_need_to_game_ai","independent_source_name":"StaffingHub article \"49% of Job Seekers Think Your AI Screening Is Biased. NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) AEDT guidance page explicitly states that **Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of its use, information about the bias audit is publicly available, and certain notices have been provided to employees or job candidates**.[1][72] The DCWP FAQ and enforcement-related documents reiterate the same requirements.[3][4][15] This matches the described audit, publication, and notice prerequisites and confirms the law’s scope as stated.","fact_id":"fairness_ll144_bias_audit_requirement","independent_source_name":"NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection – Automated Employment Decision Tools compliance guides, state that employers using AEDTs must **notify candidates and employees** that an AEDT will be used, describe the **job qualifications and characteristics** the AEDT will assess, and provide information such as how the tool will be used and the data that will be collected.[3][6][11][12] Guidance further indicates that employers must post a **summary of the most recent bias audit** on their website.[1][3][72] While some sources emphasize notice content more than data retention, several compliance summaries mention that candidates can request information about data sources and use.[11][71] Overall, the obligations around notice, explanation of assessed characteristics, and publication of audit summaries are well documented and consistent with the fact.","fact_id":"fairness_ll144_notice_transparency_requirements","independent_source_name":"NYC DCWP – AEDT materials on enforcement of Local Law 144 describe that **employers and employment agencies must conduct a bias audit of AEDTs no more than one year prior to use, provide a summary of the most recent bias audit on their website, and properly notify candidates that an AEDT will be used, how it will be used, and the data that will be collected**.[2][71] The report is framed within broader oversight concerns, and while the quoted phrase \"New Yorkers deserve a transparent hiring process\" is from a press release, that release does link these expectations to bias audits and transparency in AI vetting.[2] The fact’s description of DiNapoli’s transparency emphasis and his highlighting of LL144’s audit, posting, and notice requirements is consistent with these sources.","fact_id":"fairness_dinapoli_transparency_statement_2025","independent_source_name":"New York State Comptroller – \"Enforcement of Local Law 144\" audit page and related press academic paper \"Exploring the New York City algorithmic bias audit regime\" explains that Local Law 144 requires employers/employment agencies using AEDTs to conduct **independent bias audits** and categories**.[8][3] It also reiterates that employers, not vendors, are responsible and that audits must be updated annually.[8][3] This matches the description that LL144 mandates annual independent audits testing for disparate impact by race and gender and intersection, with reports posted and the AEDT’s distribution date** publicly available on their employment websites.[61][10] This aligns with the described employer obligations in the fact.","fact_id":"fairness_ll144_employer_obligations_deloitte","independent_source_name":"Deloitte – \"NYC Local Law 144-21 and Algorithmic The core regulatory expectation described in the fact is accurately reflected.","fact_id":"fairness_enforcement_ll144_state_audit","independent_source_name":"New York State Comptroller – \"Enforcement of Local Law 144 – Automated Employment Decision Tools\"","independent_source_url":"https://www.osc.ny.gov/state-agencies/audits/2025/12/02/enforcement-local-law-144-automated-employment-decision-tools","verdict":"CONFIRMED"},{"explanation":"The DCWP AEDT page and compliance summaries state that **Local Law 144 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using AEDTs unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of use, audit information is publicly available, and required notices have been provided**.[1][72][3] These sources paraphrase the law’s operative clause that it \"prohibits\" use absent such audits and disclosures, which aligns with the fact’s description that it \"shall be unlawful\" to use an AEDT without a recent bias audit and public summary. No contradiction appears in independent legal commentary.[7][9][14]","fact_id":"fairness_ll144_prohibits_unaudited_aedt_use","independent_source_name":"NYC DCWP – Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT) page","independent_source_url":"https://www.nyc.gov/site/dca/about/automated-employment-decision-tools.page","verdict":"CONFIRMED"},{"explanation":"The Nature Humanities and Social Sciences Communications article on AI-enabled recruitment explains that while AI can enhance recruitment efficiency, **algorithmic bias can result in discriminatory hiring practices based on gender, race, color, and personality traits** and that businesses face ethical and governance risks requiring mitigation measures.[16][17] Other ethics and business/human-rights analyses similarly highlight the risk of discrimination and reputational harm from unfair AI hiring systems.[22][30][23] This supports the statement that businesses face ethical and legal risk, including potential discrimination and damage to corporate reputation, when adopting AI-enabled hiring.","fact_id":"business_risk_of_discrimination_and_reputation_nature","independent_source_name":"Nature Humanities and Social Sciences Communications – \"Ethics and discrimination in artificial intelligence-enabled recruitment practices\"","independent_source_url":"https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-023-02079-x","verdict":"CONFIRMED"},{"explanation":"Deloitte’s commentary notes that AEDTs covered by LL144 include **data analytics, statistical modeling, machine learning, and AI that generate simplified outputs such as candidate scores, classifications, or hiring recommendations**, and that these tools are used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decisions in hiring and promotion.[61] This indicates that employers have adopted such tools for processing candidate pools and supporting decisions more efficiently.
